Other conditions associated with bone loss and osteoporo- sis include osteogenesis imperfecta (p.1083), rheumatoid arthritis (p.11), complex regional pain syndrome (p.6), chronic renal disease, and multiple myeloma (p.658); osteo- porosis may also follow organ and tissue transplantation or prolonged immobilisation. Other secondary causes in- clude the use of drugs1,5,6,10,11 such as corticosteroids (p.1491), thyroid hormones, anticonvulsants, gonadorelin analogues (p.2106), and heparin (p.1302). Risk factors for osteoporosis include non-modifiable pre- dictors of low bone mineral density (BMD), such as fe- male sex, increased age, Caucasian or Asian race, while other factors are potentially modifiable but may be inde- pendent of BMD, such as cigarette smoking, alcohol con- sumption, low body-weight, and physical inactivity. Other factors include early menopause, prolonged amenorrhoea, high caffeine intake, and nutritional deficiencies such as low calcium intake and vitamin D deficiency.1,3,6,10,13 The most important risk factors for osteoporosis-related frac- ture are a previous history of low-trauma fracture as an adult (40 years of age or older) and low BMD.1,3,4 Patients are usually asymptomatic until fractures occur,6,13 and up to two-thirds of vertebral fractures may also be asymptomatic.1,6 Fractures can result in pain, deformity (kyphosis, loss of height), and disability.1 Currently, the most reliable method of assessing osteoporosis and frac- ture risk is measurement of BMD, usually by dual energy X-ray absorptiometry.1,3,4,6,14 WHO have defined osteo- porosis as a BMD 2.5 standard deviations or more below the young adult mean, and severe or established oste- oporosis as this BMD in the presence of one or more fra- gility fractures.3 There is no universally agreed policy on screening for osteoporosis, but measurement of BMD should be considered in those thought to be at risk of oste- oporosis if the result is likely to affect treatment deci- sions.2,3,7,10,15,16 Since osteoporosis is defined in terms of BMD, the distinc- tion between clinical consequences, such as fractures, and risk, is blurred. Thus, differences between prevention and treatment are increasingly difficult to define; objectives are similar and interventions the same.3 Goals in manage- ment are to prevent fractures, optimise skeletal develop- ment to maximise peak BMD at skeletal maturity, stabilise BMD and prevent bone loss, preserve structural skeletal integrity, and to decrease morbidity and mortality from fractures.1,4 Secondary causes of osteoporosis should be identified and treated as appropriate
